abstract: Mechanistic gene-network models are widely used to rank drug-target combinations. Each ranking rests on a finite number of noisy simulations, yet the confidence that the top-ranked set is truly best in the model is rarely stated. We formulate intervention search in a stochastic network model as fixed-confidence best-arm identification and give certified search: empirical-Bernstein confidence sequences that return an {varepsilon}-optimal intervention set with probability at least 1 - 2{delta} under any sampling rule, with successive elimination and batch-parallel LUCB as sampling rules. We compare them with uniform sampling, successive halving, greedy forward selection, sequential LUCB and UGapE, and ablate each design choice, on four networks (a BeatAML-calibrated AML network and three published cancer Boolean models; 1,275 to 5,488 candidate sets) under a protocol written before the runs. All 21 certified benchmark runs returned an {varepsilon}-optimal set (exact one-sided 95% lower bound 86.7%), as did all 4,560 and 1,980 replayed runs of the comparisons, using 6.4 to 19.0 times fewer simulations than uniform sampling with the same guarantee. Elimination and the variance-adaptive radius account for most of the saving (2.1 to 34.1 and 1.3 to 3.9 times). Sequential LUCB and UGapE use fewer simulations in total but are slow on parallel hardware; batch-parallel LUCB, with as many candidates per round as workers, was at most 1% slower than successive elimination in any setting and up to 3.2 times faster, and on the three published networks used 2.0 to 3.1 times fewer simulations. Applied to AML, a search over eight drug classes returns ibrutinib + midostaurin + an ERK-inhibitor class (model score 0.710 against 0.448 untreated), which is the best set in all 15 related calibrations of the network and exceeds additive and Bliss-independence expectations.
